title: APA § 701(a): preclusion and commitment to discretion
shortTitle: APA § 701(a): preclusion and commitment to discretion
summary: APA § 701(a) recognizes statutory preclusion of review and action committed to agency discretion by law as distinct limitations.
notes:
Statutory preclusion under § 701(a)(1) asks whether Congress intended to foreclose review. Commitment to discretion under § 701(a)(2) asks whether the governing law supplies meaningful standards for assessing the decision. Possession of some discretion does not itself eliminate review for abuse: Overton Park found enforceable limits, while Chaney identified a presumptively unreviewable category of enforcement refusals.

A statute’s mandatory language and specific enforcement conditions can rebut Chaney’s presumption, as the assigned Dunlop account illustrates. The notes preserve unresolved concerns about a general policy amounting to abdication of statutory responsibilities and explain why merely labeling conduct categorical does not automatically establish reviewability. They distinguish the agency’s choice of remedy after enforcement, which can receive particularly deferential review, from whether review is available at all.

United States v. Texas (2023) illustrates overlap with standing: the Court rejected states’ attempt to compel more immigration arrests under Article III, using institutional concerns similar to those associated with nonreviewability. That standing ruling is a separate threshold doctrine and must not be treated as simply another application of § 701(a)(2).
